items.body: The Idaho Legislature unanimously approved placing the non-binding poll of state guns on the ballot through House Bill 932 this year. (Yves Adams/Getty Images) In a non-binding vote, Idaho voters nominated a lever-action rifle, dubbed the “Gun that Won the West” to be the state’s official gun. The gun, the Winchester Model 1873, had the backing from about 31% of Idaho voters, the highest share of any of the guns on the ballot in Tuesday’s general election, according to unofficial results from the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office at 12:30 p.m. Wednesday. All of Idaho’s 44 counties were reporting election results by then. A digital representation of a Winchester 1873. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office) The vote tees up a decision by the Idaho Legislature to potentially join 10 other states that have official state guns. Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. None of the six guns — placed on the ballot in a unanimous vote by the Legislature — received a majority vote. Here’s how all the guns on the list fared with voters this year: Winchester Model 1873 “Gun that Won the West” (.44-40): 31.1% of the vote, or 164,394 votes. Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30): 25.32% of the vote, or 133,859 votes. 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver, or “Peacemaker,” (.45 Colt): 15.26% of the vote, or 80,699 votes. Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06): 12.45% of the vote, or 65,818 votes. Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol (.45 ACP): 8.78% of the vote, or 46,405 votes. M1 Garand rifle (.30-06): 7.09% of the vote, or 37,500 votes. None of the guns on Idaho’s ballot have developmental ties to the state, unlike the official guns in some other states, like Utah . If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said in an interview last month that he pushed to put the question on the ballot to help drum up voter turnout. The measure, called an advisory question, had the lowest share of ballots cast of any of the statewide ballot measures. About 70% of voters cast votes in the race for the state gun, out of the more than 731,000 of voters who turned out to the polls for this election, unofficial election results show. Nearly 99% of voters cast votes on Proposition 1, a ballot initiative — which voters rejected — that sought to repeal Idaho’s near-total abortion ban. About 97% of Idaho voters cast ballots on each of the constitutional amendments: A successful one to declare English as the state’s official language , and a failed one that would’ve revoked voters’ powers to legalize marijuana and other drugs . Idaho voters turned out to vote at high rates this year in a midterm election, when voters tend to vote less. About 69% of the state’s registered voters cast ballots, early data show. But election officials expect the turnout rate to drop several points as they factor in voters who registered to vote on Election Day. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

(Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star) After months of campaigning, polling and prognostication, voters across the country had their say in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday. And despite fears about possible trouble at polling places, millions of votes were cast, mostly without incident. Voters administered a sharp reprimand to President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans, with Democrats capturing comfortable majorities in the U.S. Senate and the House. Democrats also are poised to control the majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years following major GOP losses. It was a historic day: Voters chose the first female Black governor in U.S. history in Georgia, the first Native American woman for the U.S. Senate in Minnesota, the first Black Republican governor in Florida and the first Muslim as a U.S. senator in Michigan. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1, the ballot initiative that sought to legalize abortion in the state up to fetal viability or in emergencies, and would have enumerated rights to other types of reproduct
items.body: A "Stop Prop 1" sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, held at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1, the ballot initiative that sought to legalize abortion in the state up to fetal viability or in emergencies, and would have enumerated rights to other types of reproductive healthcare. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. Wednesday. The voter-led ballot initiative received 43.68% of the vote, or 286,909 votes in the 2026 general election, as of 2:37 a.m. on Wednesday. More than 56.32% voted against it, early results showed. The proposition needed a simple majority of votes to pass. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the group formed to author and support the initiative, conceded that it did not pass in a press release sent just after 12:20 a.m. Idahoans United for Women and Families Executive Director Melanie Folwell speaks about Proposition 1 at the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings rally at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Jim Max for the Idaho Capital Sun) “This is a tremendous, frankly gutting, loss, especially for the women, families, and physicians of Idaho,” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families, said in a press release. “We will see more doctors leave the state as a result of this election. And, most urgently, women will continue to suffer needlessly under one of the most cruel abortion bans in the nation.” Election officials were still counting ballots early into Wednesday morning. Idaho’s election results do not become official until they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24. The initiative would’ve repealed Idaho’s strict abortion ban, which outlaws nearly all abortions, except to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester when a police report is provided. Idaho’s ban carries felony prison sentences and licensing penalties for doctors who perform abortions outside of the exemptions, as well as possible civil lawsuits for a minimum of $20,000. Opponents of the ballot initiative argue that it is the state’s prerogative to protect fetuses’ lives, and that Idaho’s exemptions are sufficient to protect the mother’s life. The Idaho GOP, the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise strongly opposed the initiative. Opponents formed a group called Stop Prop 1 in response to the proposed initiative. “The people of Idaho have spoken,” Stop Prop 1 communications director Mary Strow said in a press release. “They saw through the smokescreen of deception and barrage of out-of-state funded ads that sought to rewrite our laws and reshape our values. Idaho is and will always be a state that values life and protects the unborn.” Idahoans United for Women and Families formed in 2024 to explore ways to restore abortion access in the state in response to the U.S. Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022, which triggered Idaho’s bans. Idahoans United in July turned in nearly 110,000 signatures to the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office to qualify for the 2026 general election ballot. In Idaho, to qualify for the general election, supporters must collect signatures from at least 6% of the registered voters statewide and from at least 6% of the registered voters in at least 18 of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. To achieve the 6% statewide total, supporters needed 70,725 verified signatures. Its supporters argued Idaho’s laws were overreaching and potentially dangerous for pregnant women, and led to the state losing OB-GYNs. items.body: Idaho Gov. Brad Little speaks to supporters at a Republican election night watch party at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little was reelected in Tuesday’s general election and will serve a third term as the Gem State’s governor, according to the Associated Press. All other Republican candidates for statewide office were also reelected. The Associated Press called the race for Little at 10:36 p.m. Tuesday. Little addressed his supporters and several Republican officials at a downtown Boise convention hall at about 10:20 p.m. Mountain time Tuesday night, shortly before the race was officially called. “I’m humbled to have your support, grateful for your confidence, and proud to have the opportunity to continue to serve this great state,” Little told supporters Tuesday night. “Tonight’s decision results send a clear message: Idahoans want to keep moving forward. They believe in the direction the state is headed. They believe in Idaho values, and they rightfully expect us to keep delivering.” Little, a Republican from Emmett, was projected to beat his two closest challengers, Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner. As of 2:06 a.m. Mountain time Wednesday, Little had received 369,360 votes, or 57.3%, while Pickens was in second place with 206,218 votes, or 32%. Stegner was in third place, with 49,279 votes, or 7.6%. Several other candidates ran for governor as well. Libertarian Paul Sand received 10,377 votes, or 1.6%. A Constitution Party candidate who changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life received 8,649 votes, or 1.3%. And an independent named Jacob Burnett ran as a write-in candidate and had received 227 votes. Little will serve his third, four-year term as Idaho’s governor. He was first elected governor in 2018, having previously served as lieutenant governor and a member of the Idaho Senate. In addition to Little, each of Idaho’s statewide incumbent Republican officials was also leading their re-election bids Tuesday night, according to partial unofficial election results released Tuesday by the state. The Associated Press also called the race for Idaho secretary of state in favor of Republican Secretary of State Phil McGrane at 10:31 p.m. Wednesday. Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke, Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf, Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth and Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield won their re-election bids as well. Idaho Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke leads Democrat Eric Myricks Idaho’s lieutenant governor serves as president of the Idaho Senate but only votes in cases of a tie vote. The lieutenant governor also serves as acting governor while the governor is out of the state or unable to perform the duties of office. Bedke, a Republican from Oakley, held a large lead over Democratic challenger Eric Myricks of Nampa. As of 2:05 a.m. Wednesday, Bedke has received 403,994 votes, or 63.7%. Myricks had received 229,536 votes, or 36.2%. Bedke is running for his second four-year term as lieutenant governor. He previously served as the longtime speaker of the Idaho House of Representatives. (Photo courtesy of the Special Collections and Archives, Albertsons Library, Boise State University) Idahoans are encouraged to participate in a two-day event this week that honors the environmental and political legacy of Cecil Andrus, Idaho’s longest-serving governor. Share your ‘Cece story’: Boise State’s Andrus Center will host ‘History Harvest’ for book project The Andrus for Idaho: History Harvest event, hosted by the Boise State University Andrus Center, includes several panel discussions and presentations from some of the people who knew Andrus best, as well as an “Antiques Roadshow”-style History Harvest, which encourages Idahoans to bring in photos, memorabilia, artifacts, letters and oral histories from Andrus’ time in office to have them documented and archived. The two-day event will begin at 9 a.m. Friday and 9:45 a.m. Saturday at SPACE in Boise State University’s Albertsons Library, 1865 Friendship Lane on BSU’s campus. Both days of the event will go through the afternoon, and the public can join the activities at anytime throughout the day. The Andrus Center is also looking for volunteers to help with the event, including set-up beforehand, guiding visitors and helping at informational stations during the event and tear down and archival work afterward. To register as a volunteer, fill out this Google form online . Who was Cecil Andrus? Cecil Andrus, the last Democrat to serve as Idaho’s governor, died at age 85 in 2017. He was the only person to serve four terms – a nonconsecutive 14 years – as Idaho governor. But his service to the state and nation extended far beyond that one role. After serving in the U.S. Navy during the Korean War, he was concerned about the direction of Idaho’s public schools and ran for the state Senate in 1960 at just 28 years old, winning the seat. That began a longtime tenure in state politics, with his first stint as Idaho governor from 1971-1977. Serving as governor would eventually help prepare him for his role as U.S. secretary of the Interior in the Jimmy Carter administration from 1977-1981. He again was elected Idaho governor from 1987-1995. As Idaho’s population changes and grows, Emily Wakild, the Cecil D. Andrus endowed chairwoman for environment and public lands in the School of the Environment, College of Arts and Sciences, said the event is a way to bring the state’s history to life — and to capture the memories and items related to Andrus’ political life before it’s too late. Volunteers will be on-hand to scan photos, letters and other documents, while others will be available to record oral histories and personal stories about Andrus. Submissions large and small are welcome from Idahoans from all walks of life, Wakild said. “Within our history circles there’s this recognition that there are silences in archives,” Wakild said in an interview. “And there’s ways that we can account for them, but one of the best is to do a community archiving event and just simply ask people what they want to have remembered. That itself articulates, I think, some of the really strong values of the Andrus Center, which are public dialog, public interaction with lots of different perspectives and public ideas about moving forward.” Many of the people who worked with Andrus are aging, and organizers of the event hope to capture a more contextual picture of Andrus and his politics before they pass on, Wakild said. “We especially want to get people that do have those memories,” Wakild said. “But we also want people that have been here 10 minutes — people that can say, ‘oh, I moved here. items.body: Idaho Conservation League Executive Director Courtney Washburn Experienced conservationist and policy leader Courtney Washburn has been named the new executive director of the Idaho Conservation League, the league and its board of directors announced last month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Washburn succeeds previous Executive Director Justin Hayes, who announced last year he was taking a new position at the group American Rivers. The Idaho Conservation League is a more than 50-year-old nonprofit organization with a mission to protect clean air, clean water, land and wildlife. The new role represents a homecoming for Washburn, who previously served as the Idaho Conservation League’s community conservation director and statehouse lobbyist from 2006 to 2015. In her new role, Washburn is focusing on connecting and partnering with people and groups to take on the challenges of protecting Idaho. “I’m really focused on both growing the conservation community and connecting – or reconnecting, depending on how long people have lived in Idaho – with the conservation values and the actions that’s needed to protect this great state,” Washburn said in an interview Wednesday. “Progress would be to finally dispel the myth that people who care about conservation are associated with one party or another,” Washburn said. “I’d really like to see a durable kind of big tent. Everyone has a voice to speak up for their values, whether it be clean air, clean water, public lands.” “People care deeply about their state, and if you get to the core values, there are far less arguments, in my experience,” she added. Washburn also previously served as executive director for Conservation Voters for Idaho from 2015 to 2020. More recently, Washburn served as chief of staff for the city of Boise from 2020 to 2026, where she directed municipal operations, longterm planning and climate initiatives. Boise Dev reported in May that Boise Mayor Lauren McLean authorized a large severance payment for Washburn after Washburn left the city position. Data centers on public land represent a new challenge for water and wildlife habitat Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? Washburn said she opposes data centers on public lands and is working to study how they would affect water, wildlife, wildlife habitat, birds, energy use and infrastructure in Idaho. While she was visiting the site of a proposed data center south of Boise recently, Washburn said she saw 25 pronghorn. “Data centers are a particular challenge, and everyone’s kind of running to catch up,” Washburn said. “I don’t shy away from complicated issues, so I’m looking forward to digging into that,” Washburn added. items.body: The Snake River runs through Idaho Falls. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho has periodically faced serious threats to its water sovereignty from an overreaching federal government. In the early 1950s, when Len Jordan was Idaho governor, the feds wanted to build a massive dam on the Snake River in Hells Canyon. That would have usurped Idaho control of its upstream waters. Jordan stopped the proposal, opting instead for the three existing Idaho Power company dams in order to protect Idaho’s control of those waters. The next water fight occurred after I was elected as Idaho attorney general in 1982. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights Idaho Power had just received an erroneous decision from the Idaho Supreme Court, giving the company practical control of Snake River waters above its Swan Falls Dam in Ada County. Gov. John Evans and I were able to work together behind the scenes and across the political aisle to defeat that threat. When we were able to get the conflict settled to the state’s advantage, the next federal threat raised its ugly head. In December 1987, Congress was on the verge of approving legislation that would have given the feds the ability to control the flow of Snake River waters above Deer Flats Wildlife Refuge in Canyon County. The matter was being handled behind closed doors in congressional offices. When my staff members learned that a political deal was being made to compromise the state’s interests, I blew the whistle, the Idaho water community erupted in anger, and the threat was brought to a screeching halt. Anyone interested in the details can check out pages 337-345 of my book on the subject – “ A Little Dam Problem .” The latest threat to Idaho’s water sovereignty surfaced less than two months ago. Shortly after it was announced that the Idaho National Laboratory had been selected as a finalist for designation as a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus , the Trump administration launched an extremely troubling lawsuit challenging Idaho’s ability to “administer” the federal water right at the INL. In practical terms it means that, if there is a water shortage involving water rights in the INL vicinity, any reduction or mitigation would fall wholly upon the shoulders of other Idaho water users — farmers, fish producers and other folks dependent on those waters. The INL would be exempt. Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming ‘supremacy’ over our water is a gut punch to all Idahoans The lawsuit was filed against Idaho in the federal court in Boise on Sept. 11, without any attendant publicity from either side. While the allegations focus primarily upon the INL water right, the complaint seeks much broader relief. The Trump administration wants “a declaration that the Idaho Department of Water Resources lacks the authority to administer federal water rights” and “an order permanently enjoining the Director of IDWR from exercising his authority” under any state law as to the United States or its agencies. In short, the administration is asking the court to prevent Idaho from administering federal water rights anywhere within state borders. This is wholly without precedent and contrary to the determination of rights in the Snake River Basin Adjudication . The agreement settling the Swan Falls water right fight called for filing a case in state court to adjudicate all water rights to Snake River Basin waters. That is, to quantify and prioritize those rights in court proceedings. Idaho specifically sought and received approval to include all federal water rights under a federal law, called the McCarran Amendment, that permits federal claims to be determined in a state court adjudication. Idaho’s petition in the Snake River Basin Adjudication sought both adjudication and administration of water rights in the Snake River Basin. Former Gov. items.body: Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026. A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote the ballot measure days before the election. In an opinion released late Friday night , Judge Davis VanderVelde found the ads did not violate Idaho campaign finance laws and declined to keep them from being broadcast by local stations. A Republican Party operative and three board members of Too Extreme for Idaho, which opposes restoring abortion rights under Prop 1, filed their lawsuit Tuesday morning . They said the scheme used by Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), the Idaho Democratic Party and its gubernatorial candidate, Terri Pickens, concealed the true origin of who paid for the ads. IUWF, which qualified Prop 1 for the ballot, gave the Idaho Democratic Party more than $720,000 in recent weeks. The party then purchased advertising through Pickens’ campaign. All political candidates receive significant discounts on ads in the 60 days leading up to an election compared to political groups. “Ultimately, Plaintiffs’ assertion that the monies from IUWF were specifically contributed for support of Proposition 1 with the intent of concealing the original donor for such advertisements requires logical leaps that are not fully supported by the evidence,” VanderVelde wrote. Each of these transactions is publicly available in the state’s campaign finance database, which the plaintiffs cited in the evidence presented to the judge. VanderVelde said there’s also no evidence showing that IUWF still controlled the hundreds of thousands of dollars it donated to the state Democratic Party. An attorney for the defendants argued in court Thursday that the party had the final say in how any of that money was spent, which VanderVelde said was not proven otherwise by the plaintiffs. “The Court recognizes that the parties have had a short time to advance this lawsuit and that if there was additional time, additional facts may be developed by either party which could lend further credence to their claims or defenses,” he wrote. That said, the judge found there may still be outstanding legal questions about whether the ads are truly for a candidate or a proposition and whether the lower rates should apply. “However, without further law or authority significant questions remain as to what constitutes an appropriate advertisement under the law in order to qualify as an advertisement promoting a candidate.” Tom Luna, one of the plaintiffs, released a statement saying he and the three other men who brought the lawsuit disagree with the decision, but that it was important voters know who paid for the ads. “I’m sure many voters are as mad as I am about these dirty tricks. Let’s make sure we turn our frustration into action by showing up on Election Day, making our voices heard, and standing for life,” Luna said. A request for comment from the Idaho Democratic Party wasn’t immediately returned late Friday night. Memorandum Decision and Order Denying Motion For Prelimiary Injunction

items.body: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) Update: This story was updated at 5:10 p.m. on Oct. 30 with a comment from the plaintiff, Dr. Stacy Seyb. A federal appeals court panel ruled on Friday that Idaho’s abortion ban may continue to be fully enforced, including against a Boise doctor who challenged the ban’s lack of health exemption. A U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit panel ruled 2-1 to continue to block a lower court’s decision that would have prevented prosecution of maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb if he performed abortions in which he determined there were serious risks to the mother’s health or mental health. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. Seyb’s challenge, which argued Idaho’s abortion ban’s lack of exemptions to prevent serious harm to the mother’s health or death from self-harm were unconstitutional, will continue to be litigated in court. Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan said in the majority opinion that Seyb’s argument for a constitutional right to abortion as a health-saving measure or in cases of risk of self-harm were unlikely to align with the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which overturned Roe v. Wade. “We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” the majority decision said. “… Idaho has a strong interest in limiting abortions to those allowed under its law. This interest clearly outweighs the potential harm to Dr. Seyb of having to abide by Idaho’s law pending the resolution of this appeal.” Wardlaw concurred with the majority decision. Judge Marsha S. Berzon disagreed, writing that the high court’s decision only applied to elective abortions, and not when the procedure may be medically necessary or indicated. Berzon agreed with district court Judge B. Lynn Winmill, whose previous order argued there was likely a “fundamental right” to abortions to preserve the mother’s health. Berzon also argued that the risk of harm for Seyb’s patients was greater than that of the state’s. “… with the stay imposed by the majority in place, some women with serious pregnancy complications will during the pendency of this appeal be required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health,” Berzon wrote. “The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury.” Seyb said in a written statement, “Laws that criminalize abortion make pregnancy less safe.” “I will continue to advocate for the right of every patient to make important medical decisions without government interference,” he said. The conservative Christian advocacy group the Idaho Family Policy Center, which helped author Idaho’s abortion ban allowing civil lawsuits against doctors, celebrated Friday’s decision in a press release. “Pregnant mothers don’t have a constitutional right to abortion merely because they threaten to harm themselves,” Idaho Family Policy Center Blaine Conzatti said in the release. “Women in mental health crises need treatment, not abortion. items.body: The Snake River flows alongside the Idaho Falls greenbelt. (Photo courtesy of Hyo Lee/U.S. Department of Energy) Throughout history there has been one thing all Idahoans agreed on — water is the lifeblood of Idaho. Water has made our southern Idaho sagebrush country bloom with farms and ranches, and water has been crucial for the protection of our wildlife and our outdoor way of life. Protecting Idaho’s water rights from outside threats has been an article of faith — almost a religion — and any attempt by outsiders to get their hands on our water has been fighting words for all Idaho politicians regardless of political party or persuasion. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights That’s why the Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming “supremacy” over Idaho’s water serving the Idaho National Laboratory is a gut punch to the people of Idaho. But our current political leaders, unlike those throughout history, have played a role in giving the Trump administration the notion that Idaho is a lap dog for whatever the president wants by their silence and eagerness to partner with the federal government regardless of the consequences for Idahoans, their economy and their way of life. Last summer, without informing the people of Idaho, Gov. Brad Little signed a memorandum of understanding with the Trump administration hoping that the Idaho National Laboratory could become a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and accept 33 percent of all radioactive waste generated in the country . Little has not explained how this campus and taking the waste will affect our precious water supply nor how it will impact the Snake River Aquifer, which supplies a significant amount of water to our southern Idaho farms, ranches, trout farms and cities. Other than a few comments for a story published by the Idaho Capital Sun , the governor has said little about how this major initiative will affect Idaho. Our congressional delegation has also remained silent on this issue except to say the campus will bring economic prosperity and jobs to eastern Idaho. Now, through the lawsuit the Trump administration has filed in U.S. District Court, we know that the federal government views the water it receives from Idaho as its water and that Idaho has no legal right to curtail water to INL even during one of the worse drought seasons in the state’s history. The Trump administration argues that federal installations like INL are “shielded by the supremacy clause” from state regulations unless “Congress has provided clear and unambiguous authorization for such regulation.” The Trump administration also argues, as it has while promoting the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and the radioactive waste repository, that Idaho’s decision to curtail INL’s water has “safety, economic and energy consequences.” Moreover, the Trump administration says that “curtailment of INL’s water right would disrupt this national nuclear energy momentum,” another way of saying it would disrupt President Trump’s quest to build nuclear reactors across the country. But the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus is but only one issue where our water could be in jeopardy and where our governor and congressional delegation have remained silent when the future of Idaho is at stake and should be debated. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) It took two years for Chrissy Teigen to realize she’d had an abortion and not a miscarriage, longer to understand what went wrong in her pregnancy, and not until this week to realize she hadn’t fully grappled with it emotionally. Teigen, a former model and business owner, came to Idaho on Wednesday to make a final push leading up to Nov. 3 in favor of Proposition 1, the ballot measure that would restore access to abortion in Idaho. The state has a near-total ban that applies to any stage of pregnancy, with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. The initiative, if passed, would also protect access to birth control and fertility assistance treatments such as in vitro fertilization. Opponents to the measure have called the initiative too extreme because it would allow abortions up to fetal viability, which was the law in Idaho prior to the ban, with exceptions after that point when the pregnancy threatens a patient’s health or life. Prior to a rally in downtown Boise with Prop 1 volunteers and supporters, Teigen — who lived in Idaho Falls in the early 1990s — met privately at a coffee shop with 12 Idaho women who have been telling their stories for the campaign about needing abortion care in Idaho. The women sat in a circle and told brief versions of their stories: miscarriages that led to septic infections because of hesitant medical providers, travel out of state for fatal anomalies and catastrophic health complications, and memorials to the babies they lost. Nonprofit organization Idahoans United for Women and Families, which has led the campaign for the initiative, coordinated the event, and owners of Neckar Coffee donated the space and coffee. Kate Campbell spoke of her son, Remy, and the infected placenta that caused her water to break at 20 weeks and begin labor. A fetus generally can’t survive outside of the womb before 22 weeks, and every day that goes by without an abortion procedure increases the risk of a potentially life-threatening infection, which can cause organ damage and lead to fertility loss. Since Idaho’s law only allows for intervention to save a patient’s life, doctors decided not to wait until she was close to death and airlifted Campbell to Utah for care. Utah allows abortion until 18 weeks, and after that, the law includes an exception to preserve a patient’s health, not just to prevent death. “The only ‘cure,’ if you will, for an infected placenta is giving birth,” Campbell said through tears. She now has a 14-month-old daughter. Rebecca Crozier and other Idaho women sit side-by-side across from Chrissy Teigen to tell their stories of needing abortion care and being unable to access it in their home state because of the near-total ban. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) Desi Ballis had a similar story about a virus she contracted early in pregnancy that caused a fatal anomaly that also put her health in danger. A doctor at her 20-week ultrasound told her she needed to get to Utah as quickly as possible, and she and her husband, Morgan, made the five-hour drive and called multiple hospitals and clinics before they found someone who could help. “It was just horrific,” Ballis said. Read More If you miss early voting, the last chance to vote in Idaho’s general election will be in-person at the polls on Tuesday. Polls will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Idaho offers same day voter registration. By the time polls close on Election Day, absentee ballots are due to election offices. If you haven’t mailed your ballot yet, election officials encourage you to physically drop off your absentee ballot in-person at an election office or drop box. Even though the president isn’t on the ballot this year, it’s still a big election year for Idaho. All statewide offices — such as the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state superintendent, state controller and state treasurer — are up for grabs, along with three congressional seats in the U.S. House and Senate, and all 105 state legislative seats. So are local races like for county commissioners, highway district officials and even a runoff election for an Ada County judge. But perhaps the biggest race this year is Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights. That’s one of several ballot measures that voters can decide on, along with a proposed constitutional amendment that would allow only the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun. How to prepare for Idaho’s general election Visit VoteIdaho.gov , a website run by the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office, to verify your voter registration status, find your polling place and preview what your ballot will look like. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at Cathedral of the Rockies in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Trump administration is sending election monitors to Idaho’s largest county on Election Day next week, the state’s top election official confirmed Wednesday. The decision comes as the Justice Department plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors — who the DOJ says are meant to assess local compliance with federal voting rights laws — to all 50 states. That would make for a significantly expanded presence than under the Biden administration, which sent election monitors to 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections, States Newsroom reported. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, an elected Republican, said the U.S. Justice Department notified him and the Ada County Clerk’s Office, which runs the election locally, that there will be two teams in Ada County on Election Day. Ada County Clerk Trent Tripple, also a Republican, said around six election monitors who are local to Idaho will be stationed near polling places — but not inside. In a statement, the Justice Department said its election monitors in Idaho and elsewhere will be “doing the routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.” “All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate,” a spokesperson for the federal agency told the Idaho Capital Sun. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s top election official called deployment ‘routine’ The federal election monitors in Idaho, McGrane said, will be ensuring that voters have access to voting and assisting the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, such as by ensuring polling places are abiding by disability access requirements under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or ADA. McGrane called it a routine measure. He said he last remembered election monitors sent to Idaho under the Obama administration. In this file photo, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) “I’m fairly sure we’ve had it under all (presidential) administrations in some form. I can most clearly remember ADA conversations when Obama was president. But it has been routine in the past,” McGrane said in an interview. The Trump administration’s decision to expand election monitors in states for the midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake, follows recent attempts by the administration to intervene in state election processes , such as to restrict mail-in voting and obtain state voter rolls . That history has left some officials across the country concerned about the expanded election monitoring efforts. But McGrane said he isn’t worried. “I’ve seen the concerns among my peers and others nationally,” he said. “Initially, I wanted to understand and make sure what their mission was. After talking to … the new U.S. Attorney John Shirts … I feel reassured that this is something fairly routine. This is something that we’ve experienced before. And I don’t expect that voters will really even notice that it’s happening.” Tripple said he isn’t worried either. “They’ve done this before. items.body: Rebecca Crozier, 27, of Meridian, Idaho, poses in October 2026 with mementos from her baby, Haven. At 11 weeks, she received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly, and had to travel out of state to terminate the pregnancy because of her state’s near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline) MERIDIAN, Idaho — It didn’t take long for doctors to see that something was amiss with Rebecca Crozier’s pregnancy. At her eight-week ultrasound in 2025, they mentioned a possible neural tube defect, she said, but after some research, she thought it was something that could be managed or treated. “If it was a fixable problem, I was ready to quit my job and full-time care for a disabled child,” said Crozier, who is now 27. “That was something that we were prepared to do.” In the time between the two ultrasounds, she had a dream that she was carrying a baby girl, and she and her husband named her Haven. The couple lived in eastern Idaho at the time, and drove two hours to the Boise area to see the maternal-fetal medicine specialists at St. Luke’s, the state’s largest health system. Now at 11 weeks’ gestation, the specialists told her Haven had anencephaly, which occurs when the brain does not develop normally and the skull is left open, exposing brain tissue to amniotic fluid that causes the tissue to dissolve. It is a fatal condition. Rebecca Crozier takes a photo of her belly during her pregnancy before she and her husband, Kris, were told that the fetus would not survive. (Courtesy of Rebecca Crozier) “She was missing a lot of brain tissue,” Crozier recalled. “They were very clear that this baby will not go home with you. You will not take this baby home. This baby will die in the hospital if the baby survives that long.” In many states, even ones with abortion bans, Crozier would have had the option to terminate the pregnancy. But Idaho’s near-total prohibition includes no exceptions for fatal anomalies. It’s one of 11 states that do not have exceptions for anencephaly or other fatal anomalies. Next Tuesday, Idahoans will vote to determine whether the state’s near-total abortion ban should remain the law. Proposition 1, the title of the citizen-led ballot measure, would restore access to abortion until fetal viability, which was the state law before the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. Idaho is the only state this election cycle with an initiative that would restore access in a state with a ban. In Missouri, voters will consider a different initiative — to reinstate a near-total ban after passing a constitutional amendment in 2024 allowing abortion access until viability. If Idaho’s measure passes, patients like Crozier would no longer have to leave the state for an abortion. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the rate of anencephaly among newborns is about 1 in 10,000, and those babies die within a few hours or days. Most cases end in miscarriage or stillbirth; the fatal birth defect affects about 1 in 1,000 pregnancies. Crozier’s was among them. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) How competitive is the race to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate? It depends which poll you look at. According to a poll released last week by the campaign for Todd Achilles, an independent running for U.S. Senate, Republican incumbent Jim Risch has only a six-point lead over Achilles. Eight percent of voters were undecided, the poll found. The poll buoyed a claim by the Achilles campaign: Victory could be within reach. State Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “That tight margin confirms what we’re hearing in every corner of Idaho: voters are tired of career politicians controlled by their party bosses,” Achilles, 58, said in a statement with the poll’s release on Oct. 23. But the latest poll didn’t ask about support for the other two candidates in the race, which has drawn one of the most active attempts in years at unseating Risch, 83, who’s seeking a fourth, six-year-term. And Risch’s campaign polling — featuring the full line up of candidates — shows him pummeling Achilles. In the run up to Election Day in a state without much independent polling, that’s the sort of divide in polling outcomes that some pollsters expect voters to see. “Usually about this time, the candidates or the campaigns for ballot issues are publishing polls that show you that they’re going to win,” Stuart Elway, a longtime independent pollster in Washington state, said in an interview. In Idaho, independent political polls — which aren’t backed by a campaign or a special interest group — are hard to come by. They would offer a different perspective, Elway said. Stuart Elway, a retired longtime independent pollster in Washington state, speaks to journalists ahead of the 2023 legislative session in Washington. (Photo courtesy of Stuart Elway) “An independent poll that’s not sponsored by any party or candidate or interest group gives you an objective measure of how the election is going, and I think more importantly, what the people are thinking about when they’re thinking about the election,” he said. Some polling experts say that Idaho lacks independent polls because the state is reliably Republican controlled, and independent pollsters aren’t willing to invest the high funds needed to conduct reliable polling. Instead, there are candidate and special interest groups polling in Idaho, like the back and forth of polls released by the campaigns of Risch and Achilles. The poll released last week by Achilles’ campaign, conducted by VoteNexus , had info on other races — including 54% opposition for Proposition 1, a ballot initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban. In other key races, like for governor, and two U.S. House seats, Republicans were in the lead. The survey, conducted via online polls sent by text message of 700 likely Idaho voters, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. That’s because certain wording or prefaces can push people toward certain answers. If you’re looking at a poll yourself, you’ll also want to make sure that the survey is telling you its margin of error. items.body: An influenza vaccine is pictured at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Idaho health officials on Tuesday reported the state’s second flu death in the 2026-27 influenza season. The death was of a resident of Elmore County, a rural area outside Boise, who was in their 80s, the regional health agency, Central District Health, announced. The first death, reported last week, was of an Owyhee County man who was older than age 65. The deaths come as public health officials say that influenza is spreading earlier in the year than usual. In recent weeks, emergency department and urgent care visits related to the flu have been higher than they were during the same time last year, state health officials say. Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Officials at Central District Health say vaccination is the best way to reduce the risk of severe flu illness. “While most people who get the flu recover without serious complications, some groups are at higher risk for severe illness, hospitalization, and death,” said Dr. Jaime Butler-Dawson, the health district’s epidemiology program manager. “These include adults age 65 and older, pregnant people, young children, people with obesity, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes, or kidney disease.” According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season. Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Family Policy Center) Opponents of the proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to pull TV ads paid for by the Idaho Democratic Party in favor of the initiative. The conservative, Christian advocacy organization, the Idaho Family Policy Center, and leaders with a political action committee that opposes the initiative, Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, brought the lawsuit. The ballot initiative Prop 1 would repeal Idaho’s abortion ban, allowing the procedure up to viability or after in cases of emergency, enumerate rights related to a range of reproductive healthcare, and provide legal liability protections for healthcare providers who provide that type of care. The initiative will be before Idaho voters in the Nov. 3 general election. The lawsuit, filed in Canyon County court, alleges that the supporters and authors of Prop 1, a group called Idahoans United for Women and Families, paid the Idaho Democratic Party to run ads in favor of the initiative in order to pay the more favorable rates that broadcasters are required to charge to political candidates ahead of elections. The ads were run on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens. “Pro-abortion activists cheated their way into cheaper television advertisements to stump for their radical abortion ballot initiative,” Idaho Family Policy Center President Blaine Conzatti said in a written statement. “Instead of playing by the rules of the game as outlined in our state campaign finance laws, Idahoans United for Women and Families colluded with the Idaho Democratic Party to mislead voters and gain an unfair advantage. Idaho voters deserve transparency — not shell games and dirty tricks.” Idaho Democratic Party spokesperson Avery Roberts called the lawsuit “frivolous” in an email to the Idaho Capital Sun. She said it was “another attempt by opponents of Prop 1 to distract from the devastating consequences of Idaho’s extreme abortion ban.” “Women are being forced to leave the state for lifesaving medical care, and the politicians responsible have done nothing to fix it,” Roberts said. “Instead of addressing the harm this ban has caused, opponents are trying to silence the families speaking out, even after the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed our advertising complies with Idaho campaign finance laws. We won’t be intimidated into silence. Idahoans deserve to hear these families’ stories and make up their own minds on November 3.” The family policy center helped author Idaho’s law allowing family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) Chrissy Teigen will be in Boise on Wednesday to campaign in favor of Proposition 1 , which would repeal Idaho’s strict abortion ban laws and provide protections for the procedure. Proposition 1, also called the Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act , also provides protections for access to birth control, in vitro fertilization and privacy in healthcare decisions. Chrissy Teigen (Photo courtesy of Chrissy Teigen) Teigen, who is a New York Times #1 bestselling cookbook author, model, entrepreneur and advocate for maternal health, will meet privately with Idaho mothers to talk with them about how the state’s abortion ban laws have affected them. She’ll then speak at a “Yes on Prop 1” rally, to be held from noon to 1 p.m. Wednesday at Treefort Music Hall, to encourage Idahoans to cast their ballots during the final days of early voting. The Treefort Music Hall is located at 722 W. Broad St. in Downtown Boise, and the rally is open to the public. Idahoans will decide the outcome of Proposition 1 during the Nov. 3 general election. It would take a simple majority of “yes” votes across the state to approve Prop 1. Under Idaho’s abortion ban laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors in Idaho can be sued for a minimum of $20,000 and be criminally prosecuted for performing an abortion. “In September 2020, Teigen underwent a medically necessary abortion at 20 weeks after experiencing a partial placental abruption, a serious pregnancy complication that put her health at risk,” a press release announcing Teigen’s appearance said. “The pregnancy was deeply wanted, but the baby was not expected to survive, and continuing the pregnancy posed serious risks to Teigen’s health.” Idaho’s abortion ban laws do not carve out an exception to protect a mother’s health, and instead only has an exception to prevent her death. items.body: The Idaho State Capitol building as seen on Jan. 23, 2024, in Boise. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho lawmakers will weigh whether to fund several drug-prevention and treatment projects, totaling over $3 million, through the state’s endowment fund from tobacco lawsuit settlement money. The legislative Joint Millennium Fund Committee, which oversees the endowment, heard 10 proposals Friday for use of the settlement money, which must go toward drug and alcohol prevention. As of Sept. 30, the fund’s balance was nearly $43.5 million — however, some of the previously approved projects hadn’t yet been funded, according to Senior Budget and Policy Analyst Janica Bisharat. The committee is focused particularly on youth prevention and cessation in approving use of the fund for projects. Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, (right) chats with Sen. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle, on the Senate floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “I am laser-focused on prevention,” committee co-Chair Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, said Friday. “I have three deaths in my family already, and two or three more that are getting close. I’ve seen abuse. I’ve seen the problem, and as long as I have this position, I’m gonna focus on that. And that’s the focus of our group here is prevention.” The committee did not decide on its recommended projects to fund. The funding would need final approval from legislative budget writers on the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee during the legislative session, which begins in January. Here are the proposed projects lawmakers heard Friday: Recovery Idaho asks for $32,780 to create a certification process for recovery centers The nonprofit Recovery Idaho sought just under $33,000 to create a voluntary accreditation program for recovery centers statewide. Recovery centers provide treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and also often provide additional support for clients in treatment. “The problem right now is that the recovery community centers throughout the state are very well intentioned, but there’s a fair amount of variation and maybe not enough tracking of what exactly happens and what those outcomes are,” Andra Smith Hansen, a Recovery Idaho board member, told the committee members. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The director of Idaho’s largest state agency will step down by the end of the year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron told employees in a letter she’d be stepping back to provide more support to her family, Boise State Public Radio first reported. Gov. Brad Little’s communication director, Emily Callihan, told BSPR that Charron’s father faced “significant health challenges.” “This has not been an easy decision,” Charron wrote in the letter to employees. “The past year has brought significant challenges for my family, and I realize that they need more of my time, attention, and support. Family has always been important to me, and right now, being there for mine needs to be my priority.” Charron’s last day has not been finalized, and it’s unclear who will serve as interim director when she leaves. Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Little appointed Charron as director in July 2025, and she officially stepped into the post in September last year, after previously serving as the agency’s top Medicaid official since 2021, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. “I want to thank Juliet Charron for her outstanding service as Health and Welfare Director,” Little said in a written statement to the Sun. “Under her leadership, the department made meaningful progress in strengthening child welfare prevention, preparing to distribute nearly $200 million in Rural Health Transformation funding in the coming months as part of nearly $1 billion over five years, and improving compliance, accountability, and program outcomes. I appreciate her commitment to serving Idahoans and look forward to announcing new leadership for the state’s largest agency before the end of the year.” Health and Welfare spokesman AJ McWhorter told the Sun the agency had “a number of vacancies in some key positions for a variety of unrelated reasons, including external opportunities, retirements, and personal and family reasons.” “The Governor’s Office will announce a new director at a later date,” McWhorter said. “DHW is hiring for the other positions, and we encourage qualified people to apply. We will continue to focus on the work and provide quality, efficient, and effective services for the people of Idaho.” Before joining Idaho’s health agency, Charron held leadership positions in the Texas Medicaid program and with the Texas Office of Inspector General. She also worked in government programs and “compliance roles” for a community-based health plan in Arizona, according to her biography . Charron leaves Idaho’s largest agency with the biggest budget The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare runs public assistance programs like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the Women and Infant Children program. The health department also provides public health services, regulates long-term care facilities, runs the state’s mental health hospitals, provides child welfare and provides services for people with developmental disabilities. The agency’s total budget is more than $5 billion of mostly federal funds. The full transition to managed care oversight of Medicaid is expected to happen by 2030. Charron has also overseen the influx of federal funds from the Rural Health Transformation Grant. items.body: Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios, but high costs to build such projects can create barriers. (Photo by Gregory Thomas/USDA) High costs and lengthy permitting processes are two of the barriers to bringing nuclear-powered electricity to customers in Idaho, officials from three electrical utilities told state regulators during a public forum outside of Boise on Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios. However, the high cost to build nuclear power projects, the absence of price certainty and permitting processes that can stretch for 10 years or longer do not align with state regulators’ “least cost, least risk” mandate. “When I think of the benefits of nuclear, I think diversity is a huge part of it,” Idaho Power Chief Operating Officer Adam Richins said. “Obviously, it’s dispatchable clean energy, which really doesn’t exist besides nuclear.” Adam Richins was named Idaho Power’s executive vice president and chief operating officer in February 2026 after previously serving in other roles at the utility. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Power) “On the other side of the spectrum … right now we don’t know how much it’s going to cost, and obviously when you talk about ‘least cost, least risk,’ that is very important,” Richins said. For example, Richins said the expansion of Plant Vogtle nuclear power plant in Georgia ran over budget by $16 billion to $21 billion. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission sets rates and regulates investor-owned and privately-owned utilities that provide electricity, gas, water or some telephone services for a profit. The three members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, or PUC for short, are appointed by the governor. None of the three companies use nuclear in their energy mix. But Rocky Mountain Power officials recently announced a 40-year power purchase agreement to buy electricity from a TerraPower nuclear power plant that is being built in Kemmerer, Wyoming. The Wyoming plant is being built at the site of a coal plant that is being retired, with about $2 billion in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Energy supporting the project. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission did not have any specific nuclear energy proposals under consideration during Tuesday’s forum and did not take any action. “The primary purpose of this opportunity for us is to listen to each and every one (of the utilities participating in the forum),” Idaho PUC Chairman Edward Lodge said. Democratic challenger Shawn Keenan is again challenging Republican incumbent Secretary of State Phil McGrane , who widely defeated Keenan in the 2022 election. Keenan, a mortgage broker and loan officer who lives in Coeur d’Alene, says he’s running again to avoid and combat election misinformation. McGrane, a seasoned Idaho election official seeking a second term, says he’s running on a track record of keeping elections secure and improving access to election information. The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. The secretary of state is a statewide office that oversees elections in the state, manages campaign finance compliance and transparency, and maintains records on businesses. The secretary of state also serves on the Land Board, which manages the state’s endowment lands. The secretary of state serves a four-year term and earns an annual salary of $128,690. In a Republican-controlled state, Keenan’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. Keenan runs a nonprofit, called the North Idaho Kindness Project, that focuses on fostering acts of kindness — like love letters around Valentine’s Day and kindness tokens, which his group encourages people to hand out to people they see doing random acts of kindness. Educational exhibits are placed along the trail to provide information. (Photo courtesy of the National Park Service) The Friends of Minidoka nonprofit will host its 2026 symposium, which will feature a film screening, legal discussion and lecture, “to consider the enduring importance of due process, equal protection, and civic engagement in protecting our civil liberties and strengthening democracy,” according to a press release from the organization. The 2026 Civil Liberties Symposium, titled Law, Civil Liberties, and the Continuing Pursuit of Justice: From Wayne Collins to Today, will examine how “the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II continues to inform contemporary debates surrounding immigration, detention, national security, and constitutional rights,” the press release said. In 1942, the Minidoka War Relocation Center was constructed in Jerome County at Hunt, Idaho. Locally, it was known as “Hunt Camp.” While in operation, the site was the seventh largest city in Idaho, incarcerating nearly 9,400 people at its peak population. (Photo courtesy of the National Archives and Records Administration) The series begins Thursday with a screening of “Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman,” a 30-minute documentary about the San Francisco attorney who spent more than two decades defending Japanese Americans who renounced their U.S. citizenship under duress while imprisoned at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II. The screening will be followed by a discussion with Emily Croston, staff attorney with the ACLU of Idaho, and Wendy Olson, former U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho and chairwoman of the Idaho State Bar’s Diversity Section. On Nov. 5, the group will host its 2026 distinguished lecture: “Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do,” presented by Kari Hong, the director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law. Drawing on her experience as an immigration attorney, public interest lawyer, and legal scholar, Hong will examine the history and present-day realities of immigration enforcement and detention, along with opportunities to protect the rights of affected individuals. The lecture will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the audience. The symposium concludes Dec. 8 with an online presentation of Hong’s distinguished lecture, offering another opportunity for community members to participate and engage with these issues. “History reminds us that civil liberties can be threatened when fear and claims of national security are used to justify the erosion of constitutional protections,” said Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka. “By bringing historical perspectives into conversation with today’s legal challenges, the Civil Liberties Symposium creates opportunities for our community to learn, ask difficult questions, and consider our shared responsibility to uphold justice.” All events are free and open to the public, with registration required. items.body: An orange "detour ahead" sign alerts motorists of a new route around new housing construction in Boise in summer 2026. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s newly approved Opportunity Zones could help bring more housing, businesses and jobs to communities across the state. The attraction for investors is the potential tax savings. This month, Idaho Commerce announced that the U.S. Treasury approved 25 zones, including areas in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls. The new Opportunity Zone designations take effect Jan. 1. An Opportunity Zone is a designated area where the federal government offers tax benefits to encourage private investment. The idea is straightforward: give investors a financial reason to put money into communities that could benefit from more economic activity. In Boise, the five areas identified by the city are Downtown, Shoreline, University District, South Boise Village and West Boise . These are general descriptions of the selected areas. The actual boundaries determine whether a particular property is included. In North Idaho, the officially designated list includes parts of Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls, as well as areas around Blanchard and Kellogg, Smelterville and Wardner. Other designated communities include Caldwell, Garden City, Nampa, Pocatello and Twin Falls. The state’s announcement provides the complete list and a link to look up the boundaries . The program connects investors with projects that need money. An investor who sells stock, real estate or a business at a profit may face a tax bill on that gain. By investing an eligible gain through a special investment vehicle called a Qualified Opportunity Fund, the investor may receive tax benefits. The fund puts that money into qualifying property or businesses within a zone. The IRS explains the basic structure here . Imagine a business owner who sells a company and wants to invest some of the profit. Across town, a developer wants to turn an underused property into apartments with shops on the ground floor. If the project is in an Opportunity Zone and meets the program’s requirements, an Opportunity Fund could connect that investor’s money with the development. The investor receives an ownership interest, and the project receives money to help move forward. Under the new rules beginning in 2027, a qualifying investor generally can delay tax on the invested gain for five years and reduce the amount of that gain subject to tax. Holding the investment for at least 10 years may also allow the investor to avoid federal tax on qualifying growth in the investment’s value. Coeur d’Alene also offers a potential partnership story. Idaho Capital Sun reported that Kootenai County and the Coeur d’Alene Tribe both sought designation for the local tract. The application summary identified vacant tribal land as an opportunity for investment involving the Tribe, local governments, and private developers. That possibility deserves attention, although the designation itself does not establish a finalized development partnership. For investors, those benefits can make a long-term investment more attractive. For developers and business owners, the program can help attract money from people willing to wait for a project to mature. That could support a new apartment building, the redevelopment of an older commercial property, or the expansion of a qualifying business. Residents may benefit from additional homes, employment, and services. Those outcomes are possibilities, not promises. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: Work continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, on April 17, 2026. Today’s data center buildout has become the largest industrial boom since the railroad era of the 19th century, with $10 trillion in investment and almost twice the economic impact. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) The sheer size of investment in data centers is drawing concern as it surpasses all other historical booms and crowds out other more job-creating ventures. Until now, no industry had driven the U.S. economy with such force since the railroad expansion of the late 1800s, when titans battled one another to lay the transcontinental tracks that would connect America from coast to coast. Railroads in the 19 th century consumed about $173 billion in today’s dollars and created more than 2% of the nation’s annual economic output (GDP) over 20 years. Today’s data center buildout will dwarf that amount, with $10 trillion in investment, and now have almost twice the economic impact — nearly 4% of GDP. That’s according to a report created by a Columbia Business School professor, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. States are starting to feel left out of the windfall, many having granted tax exemptions before the boom. Years ago, before artificial intelligence prompted a tsunami of building, states typically welcomed data centers supporting internet traffic, offering tax abatements and other perks. Many officials now are rethinking that approach as tax revenues take a bigger hit and high energy demands take a toll on affordability. Nevada , for instance, trimmed tax abatements and will ask data centers to agree to foot the bill for energy and water demands, in a September executive order from Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. States where data center costs will be concentrated over the three years are Texas ($638 billion), Virginia ($249 billion), Ohio ($169 billion) and Georgia ($160 billion), according to projections from Industrial Info Resources, a market intelligence firm. Southern states dominate the landscape for the number of data centers planned, with large numbers also proposed in Arizona, California, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington state, according to a Pew Research Center report in April. The profitability of AI has yet to catch up with the expense of the buildout. “It is not a pretty picture right now,” said IIR’s senior vice president of research, David Pickering. “I think it will become profitable once things settle down a bit and more legislation is put in place to regulate how we handle AI. “The big players will no doubt find a way to make it profitable,” he said. There are signs the staggering cost of data centers is crowding out other investments such as housing. Over the past two years new construction value for data centers has more than doubled to $85 billion annually, while all other construction value has dropped 8%, according to a Stateline analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data as of August. As new data center value grew by $48 billion since 2024, new houses and apartments dropped by $29 billion, according to the data. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s newly refurbished replica of the Liberty Bell will be rededicated Nov. 23 during ceremonies at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise, Idaho State Historical Society Executive Director Janet Gallimore said Thursday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE In January, the bell was sent to the Bell Foundry Christoph in Charleston, S.C. for cleaning and refurbishing in connection with this year’s America250 celebrations in Idaho. The refurbished Liberty Bell made it back to the Idaho State Capitol in July for the America250 celebration, and then was sent on a tour of cities and towns in all 44 Idaho counties so that school children and the public could see and ring the bell. At the completion of the statewide tour, the Liberty Bell will return to Boise for a free, public rededication ceremony at noon on Nov. 23. During those ceremonies, the Liberty Bell will be reinstalled at its home on the front steps of the Idaho State Capitol. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US The America250 in Idaho Advisory Council in December voted to spend up to $28,500 to clean and refurbish the Liberty Bell. During the America250 in Idaho Advisory Council’s meeting on Thursday, Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth floated the idea of installing a new liberty fountain in Idaho as a permanent landmark for this year’s America250 celebration. Ellsworth, who said she has already had Zoom meetings with state legislators on the subject, estimated the liberty fountain would cost $1 million, and encouraged the state to fundraise to generate the money for the fountain. “This is the gift that we want to give a lasting legacy to Idaho about America250,” Ellsworth said. Ellsworth did not say where the liberty fountain might be built. The advisory council did not take any action on the liberty fountain Thursday, but members encouraged Ellsworth to see if all the different officials and stakeholders who would need to support the project are on board and then report back during the council’s next meeting, which is tentatively scheduled for Dec. 10.

(Photo courtesy of Alliance for Youth Action) Editor’s Note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th . Boise State University senior Cade Syvock opposes abortion. As president of the school’s chapter of the conservative group Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late activist Charlie Kirk, Syvock helped coordinate anti-abortion protests on campus. But he’s not spending much time this fall campaigning against an Idaho ballot initiative that would restore abortion access. Not for lack of interest — he calls the proposed law “very, very extreme” because it allows abortions after viability in certain emergency cases — but because of pressing economic issues he’d rather be working on. “It’s not like everybody’s going out and getting abortions 24/7, but everybody is trying to find a home,” Syvock said. In Idaho and Missouri, where voters will decide the future of abortion access on Nov. 3, campaigns are trying to reach a generation dealing with rising living costs and skepticism toward politics. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue. But for many others, it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. Idaho’s initiative would restore abortion access. Missouri’s measure seeks to reinstate a near-total ban jettisoned by voters two years ago. People pushing for and against both measures are making their appeals to young voters, using social media and canvassing to increase turnout on Election Day, but they’re competing against other issues for Generation Z’s attention. “I’m not saying that the abortion stuff is any less important than housing, but I think in terms of what young people are focusing on right now, it’s definitely dropped a little bit,” Syvock said. Gen Z politicians who want to make a change grapple with parties that aren’t always ready for them In most elections, it’s difficult for campaigns to achieve high turnout among young voters, especially in between presidential election cycles. Less than half of the 40 million Gen Z Americans between ages 18 and 29 who were eligible to vote in 2024 cast a ballot, a study by the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University found. This year, the number of eligible Gen Z-age voters is estimated at nearly 50 million. But there are some signs that turnout could be higher this year. Nonpartisan youth vote organization The Civics Center noted a significant increase in voter registration among 18-year-olds compared with the 2022 midterms, from 35% to 42%. And the Tufts survey points out that there are many signs Gen Z is active and engaged on political subjects, but that connecting issues to candidates and ballot questions is the challenge. The majority of Gen Z adults support abortion access, according to a September poll from The 19th and YouGov. But there’s a gender gap: Women were more likely than men to say abortion should be always or mostly legal, 69% to 51%. Almost half of men versus 31% of women say it should be mostly or always illegal. The number of Generation Z Missourians who got involved in the 2024 initiative petition is not available, but more than 110,000 Idahoans signed the petition to put abortion access on the state ballot. About 7% of those signatures came from people between the ages of 18 and 25, and twice as many of those signatures came from women than from men. But some organizing efforts are made more difficult by local politics as well as increasing costs for food, housing and transportation. The 19th/YouGov poll found that 21% of Gen Z adults were worried about their ability to pay for groceries and 34% were somewhat worried.
